title: Distributions, random state and Monte Carlo evidence
outcome: Use explicit random generators, compare simulation with analytic quantities and preserve the distinction between numerical and sampling uncertainty.
key_terms: An explicit generator such as `Xoshiro(42)` passed to `rand`, so a run reproduces exactly the same draws.
A Distributions.jl value such as `Normal(2, 3)` that supplies methods like `rand`, `cdf` and `quantile`.
The sampling uncertainty of a simulated mean, estimated as the standard deviation divided by the square root of the draw count.
The chance that a variable exceeds a threshold, computed with `ccdf` or with `logccdf` when the value is tiny.
The classroom helper module that captures one bounded Plotly figure with a description and an exact data table.
approach: Make every random draw come from a named generator such as `Xoshiro(42)` and compare simulated summaries with exact distribution quantities. Worked example A samples 4000 draws from `Normal(2, 3)` and judges the sample mean with the scale 3 divided by sqrt(4000). Worked example B compares `Binomial(10, 0.2)` frequencies with exact masses.

exercises.title: State the parameterization
exercises.hint: The second argument is standard deviation.
exercises.answer: A familiar parameter name should be checked against the actual distribution API.
exercises.why: Distributions.jl parameterizes `Normal(μ, σ)` by standard deviation, so `Normal(2, 3)` has mean 2 and variance 9.
exercises.wrong: Reading the second argument as variance, as some textbooks write N(μ, σ²), predicts variance 3 and a much narrower spread.

exercises.title: Reproduce a sequence
exercises.task: Create two generators with the same seed and sample the same distribution.
exercises.expected: They produce equal arrays in the stated runtime.
exercises.answer: This demonstrates reproducibility under the current implementation, not a universal cross-version promise.
exercises.why: Two `Xoshiro(42)` generators start in the same state, so drawing 4000 values from each yields identical arrays in this runtime.
exercises.wrong: Relying on the global default generator lets any earlier call elsewhere in the script change the sequence.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `first == second`; the reference also asserts `rand(Xoshiro(3), 3) == before`.

exercises.title: Advance the generator
exercises.task: Draw twice from one generator object.
exercises.expected: Its state advances and the arrays differ in the fixture.
exercises.hint: A seed initializes state; it is not reapplied on every call.
exercises.answer: Reusing or recreating a generator defines different sampling procedures.
exercises.why: Each call to `rand(generator, 3)` advances the same generator, so the second batch continues the stream rather than repeating it.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the seed to be applied again on every call predicts equal batches and misreads how generator state works.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `before != after` for consecutive draws from one `Xoshiro(3)`.

exercises.title: Scale Monte Carlo work
exercises.task: Increase the draw count by a factor of 4 under independent sampling.
exercises.expected: The theoretical mean standard-error scale halves.
exercises.hint: Use sigma divided by square root of n.
exercises.answer: An individual realization can still deviate unpredictably; the scaling is a statement about the sampling model.
exercises.why: The standard error of the mean is σ divided by sqrt(n), so four times the draws multiplies it by 1/2.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the error to shrink by four confuses variance scaling with standard-error scaling.
exercises.verify: Compute `3 / sqrt(4000)` and `3 / sqrt(16000)` and confirm the ratio is exactly 2.

exercises.title: Inspect an extreme tail
exercises.task: Compare a survival-function calculation with naive subtraction.
exercises.expected: A stable tail API retains a small positive probability.
exercises.hint: Avoid cancellation before taking a logarithm.
exercises.answer: Probability APIs have different numerical roles even when algebraic formulas look equivalent.
exercises.why: At z = 10, `cdf(Normal(), 10)` rounds to 1.0 in `Float64`, so `1 - cdf` is 0, while `ccdf` computes the tiny tail directly.
exercises.wrong: Taking `log(1 - cdf(Normal(), 10))` gives negative infinity and breaks any likelihood that uses it.
exercises.verify: Example B checks that `ccdf(Normal(), 10.0)` lies between the two Mills-ratio bounds and that `logccdf` is finite.

exercises.title: Interpret the plot
exercises.task: Compare empirical frequencies with the exact Binomial masses.
exercises.expected: Finite simulated frequencies fluctuate around the model probabilities.
exercises.hint: Keep the sample size and model assumptions visible.
exercises.answer: The chart is a mechanism demonstration and does not establish a real population distribution.
exercises.why: Two thousand draws give empirical frequencies that sum to 1 and scatter around the exact masses, such as `pdf(0) = 0.8^10`.
exercises.wrong: Treating a gap between a bar and its marker as a model failure ignores the sampling noise expected at this size.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `sum(empirical) ≈ 1` and `pdf(distribution, 0) ≈ 0.8^10`; compare each gap with sqrt(p(1-p)/2000).

checks_note: Closed forms anchor these checks: the standard normal is symmetric, so its cdf at 0 is 0.5 and its median is 0, and the log density at 0 is minus half of log 2 pi. A negative scale raises `DomainError`. The generator lines show that consecutive draws from one stream differ, while a fresh `Xoshiro(3)` reproduces the first three numbers.
